papers.title: The Upper Clique Transversal Problem: Hardness and Algorithms
papers.abstract: A clique transversal in a graph is a set of vertices intersecting all maximal cliques. The problem of determining the minimum size of a clique transversal has received considerable attention in the literature. In this paper, we initiate the study of the ''upper'' variant of this parameter, the upper clique transversal number, defined as the maximum size of a minimal clique transversal. We investigate this parameter from the algorithmic and complexity points of view, with a focus on various graph classes. We show that the corresponding decision problem is NP-complete in the classes of chordal graphs, chordal bipartite graphs, cubic planar bipartite graphs, and line graphs of bipartite graphs, but solvable in linear time in the classes of split graphs, proper interval graphs, and cographs, and in polynomial time for graphs of bounded cliquewidth. We conclude the paper with a number of open questions.

papers.title: Maximal Linear Arrangement is NP complete on Bipartite Graphs
papers.abstract: The linear arrangement of a simple graph $G = (V,E)$ is a bijective labeling $\pi$ of the vertices of $G$ to the set $\{1, \ldots, n\}$. The maximum linear arrangement ($\texttt{maxLA}$) problem is to determine whether $G$ has a labeling such that the sum of labels across $G$'s edges, $\sum_{uv \in E} |\pi(u) - \pi(v)|$, is at least a given value $k$. Minimum linear arrangement ($\texttt{minLA}$) is defined analogously. Both $\texttt{maxLA}$ and $\texttt{minLA}$ are known to be NP complete for general graphs. $\texttt{minLA}$ has shown to be NP complete for bipartite graphs by Evans and Shiloah in 1975. It has been an open problem whether the same holds for $\texttt{maxLA}$. In this paper we prove that $\texttt{maxLA}$ is NP complete for bipartite graphs.

papers.title: Detection and Construction of Small Blocking Sets via Critical Independent Sets and Matching Decomposition
papers.abstract: The small blocking set detection and construction problem asks whether a given connected simple graph contains a nonempty independent set whose cardinality equals the size of its neighborhood and is strictly less than half the number of vertices, and, if so, how to construct such a set. Previous work characterized restless explorability in vertex-permuted temporal graphs using small blocking sets, but left the computational complexity of detecting their existence as an open problem. We give a polynomial-time algorithm for detection and construction. Specifically, we first compute a maximum-cardinality critical independent set and use its difference and cardinality to handle the cases that admit an immediate solution. In the remaining boundary case, where the critical difference is zero and the selected independent set contains exactly half the vertices, we establish a projection theorem using a perfect matching and neighborhood counting: the graph contains a small blocking set if and only if the selected independent set contains a nonempty proper tight subset. We then use matching contraction to translate the tight-subset condition into the absence of arcs leaving a vertex subset in an auxiliary digraph. This yields a strong-connectivity test for the existence of a small blocking set and, when one exists, a construction based on a sink strongly connected component. The result resolves the open complexity question for small blocking set detection and provides an explicit construction algorithm.

papers.title: Equitable Subpartitionability Does Not Characterize Box-TDI Polyhedra
papers.abstract: Equitable subpartitionability (ESP) is a sufficient condition for an integral system to be box-totally dual integral. We show that the converse fails even when alternative descriptions of the same polyhedron are allowed. We provide a geometrical characterization of polyhedra that can be described by ESP systems in terms of normal cones. We construct a four-dimensional integer polytope described by a totally equimodular matrix that admits no integral ESP description. This answers negatively a previously posed question by the same authors.

papers.title: Polynomial directed treewidth forces a large bramble with congestion two
papers.abstract: Brambles of constant congestion in directed graphs have interesting structural and algorithmic applications, and it is desirable to find the smallest function $f_c(k)$ such that if a digraph has directed treewidth at least $f_c(k)$, then it contains a bramble of size at least $k$ and congestion at most $c$. By the Directed Grid Theorem of Kawarabayashi and Kreutzer [STOC 2015], such a function $f_c(k)$ exists for every value $c \geq 2$ of the congestion. However, even using the recent improvements due to Hatzel et al. [FOCS 2024], the resulting function is a power tower of height $22$. Recently, Masa\v{r}\'ik et al. [SIAM J. Discrete Math. 2022] proved that, for congestion $8$, the function $f_8(k)$ can be made polynomial; more precisely, they showed that $f_8(k) = \mathcal{O}(k^{48} \cdot \log^{13} k)$. They asked whether it is possible to decrease the congestion, ideally to $2$, even at the cost of a higher polynomial function. In this work we answer their question affirmatively with the best possible value of the congestion, by proving that $f_2(k) = \mathcal{O}(k^{96}\cdot \log^{23} k)$. We also obtain smaller polynomials for higher congestion, namely $f_4(k) = \mathcal{O}(k^{72} \cdot \log^{21} k)$ and $f_6(k) = \mathcal{O}(k^{66} \cdot \log^{18} k)$. Our results are inspired by the proof for congestion $8$, which we improve by introducing walkages. Walkages allow us to avoid technicalities of the original proof by translating ideas due to Reed and Wood [Eur. J. Comb. 2012] that work for undirected graphs to the directed setting. Our proofs are constructive and naturally yield polynomial-time algorithms to find the brambles assuming a certificate for large directed treewidth is given. Moreover, we discuss algorithmic applications of our results for the Directed Disjoint Paths with Congestion problem, and to half-integral packings of subgraphs with large directed treewidth.

papers.title: The Stable Marriage Polytope is Box-Totally Dual Integral
papers.abstract: A stable matching in a bipartite preference system is a matching that has no unmatched pair whose endpoints both prefer each other to their current assignments. Rothblum gave a linear description of the stable marriage polytope, the convex hull of the incidence vectors of stable matchings. We prove that this polytope is box-totally dual integral. The proof uses the affine representation of the stable marriage polytope as an order polytope together with the matricial characterization of box-TDI polyhedra. Since Kiraly and Pap proved that Rothblum's description is totally dual integral, our result further implies that Rothblum's system is box-totally dual integral.

papers.title: The Game Chromatic Number of Complete Multipartite Graphs
papers.abstract: In this paper we investigate the game chromatic number for complete multipartite graphs. Our results consist of two findings: (1) building on Dunn's strategies for equal-sized parts, we determine the closed-form formulas for the game chromatic number for all complete multipartite graphs without singletons, with respective optimal strategies for Alice and Bob, (2) for an explicit list of part sizes, we give an exact algorithm that computes the game chromatic number in polynomial time and allows for reconstructing an optimal strategy for both players. Additionally, we provide counterexamples to earlier, partial formulas for complete multipartite graphs with singletons and large equal-sized parts.

papers.title: The Smallest String Attractors of Fibonacci, Period-Doubling, and Thue--Morse Words
papers.abstract: A string attractor of a string $T[1..|T|]$ is a set of positions $\Gamma$ of $T$ such that any nonempty substring $w$ of $T$ has an occurrence that crosses a position in $\Gamma$, i.e., there is a position $i$ such that $w = T[i..i+|w|-1]$ and the intersection $[i,i+|w|-1]\cap \Gamma$ is nonempty. The size of the smallest string attractor of Fibonacci words and period-doubling words of length at least $2$ is known to be $2$. The size of the smallest string attractor of Thue--Morse words of length at least $25$ is known to be $4$. We completely characterize the set of all smallest string attractors of Fibonacci words, period-doubling words, and Thue--Morse words. For Fibonacci words, we show a recursive formula describing the $2^{n-4} + 2^{\lceil n/2 \rceil - 2}$ distinct position pairs that are the smallest string attractors of the $n$th Fibonacci word for $n \geq 7$. For period-doubling words, we show a formula describing the two distinct position pairs that are the smallest string attractors of the $n$th period-doubling word for $n\geq 2$. For Thue--Morse words, we show a formula describing the 32 sets of four positions that are the smallest string attractors of the $n$th Thue--Morse word for $n\geq 6$. Our results show that strings with the same smallest attractor size can have a drastically different number of distinct smallest attractors.

papers.title: Hamilton paths and cycles in flip graphs of (almost-)perfect matchings
papers.abstract: We consider the set of matchings of a graph and a local change operation, called a flip, between them. In the combinatorial setting, the base graphs are either complete graphs or complete bipartite graphs, and in the geometric setting, the graphs are embedded on point sets in the plane, with the requirement that edges must be drawn as straight lines and must not cross. For base graphs with an even number of vertices, we consider perfect matchings, i.e., all vertices are matched, and for base graphs with an odd number of vertices, we consider almost-perfect matchings, i.e., all but one vertex of the graph are matched. A 2-flip between two perfect matchings exchanges two edges, and a 1-flip between two almost-perfect matchings exchanges one edge. The corresponding flip graph has the set of perfect or almost-perfect matchings as vertices, with pairs of them connected by an edge if they differ in a 2-flip or 1-flip, respectively. In this work, we provide a comprehensive picture of Hamiltonicity properties of these flip graphs. We prove that the flip graphs in the combinatorial setting are Hamilton-connected, i.e., they admit a Hamilton path between any two vertices, or, if the flip graphs are bipartite, we prove that they are Hamilton-laceable, i.e., they admit a Hamilton path between any two vertices from different partition classes. In the geometric setting, we prove that any path in them misses exponentially many vertices, in particular, they have no Hamilton paths or cycles. For points in convex position and almost-perfect matchings under 1-flips, we complement this by constructing a cycle in the flip graph that visits almost all vertices.

papers.title: The Integrality Gap of the Traveling Salesman Problem is $4/3$ if the LP Solution Has at Most $n+6$ Non-zero Components
papers.abstract: We address the classical Dantzig - Fulkerson - Johnson formulation of the symmetric metric Traveling Salesman Problem and study the integrality gap of its linear relaxation, namely the Subtour Elimination Problem (SEP). This integrality gap is conjectured to be 4/3. We prove that, when solving a problem on n nodes, if the optimal SEP solution has at most n + 6 non-zero components, then the conjecture is true. To establish this result, we devise a new methodology that combines theoretical analysis and computational verification.

papers.title: Differentiable Repairability & Mutations for Scalable Combinatorial Optimization
papers.abstract: Combinatorial optimization problems such as Maximum Independent Set (MIS) and Maximum Cut (MaxCut) arise across a wide range of applications, yet solving large-scale instances remains computationally challenging. While discrete local-search procedures can produce high-quality solutions, their inherently sequential and iterative nature can become increasingly expensive as problem size and density grow. In this paper, we present a differentiable perspective on combinatorial optimization that leverages continuous relaxation with parallelizable gradient-based updates to improve scalability while reducing dependence on discrete local search. More specifically, for MIS, we show that solutions that remain repairable through a discrete (1,2)-swap can nevertheless be fixed points of projected gradient ascent, revealing a fundamental limitation of purely local gradient dynamics. For MaxCut, we develop a new quadratic formulation whose landscape provably allows projected gradient ascent to escape 1-flip-repairable solutions while ensuring binary local maximizers. Building on these insights, and inspired by discrete perturb-and-improve methods, we introduce a framework that combines projected gradient ascent with differentiable mutations (partial resets) to efficiently explore new regions of the solution space}. Experimental results on MIS and MaxCut demonstrate the potential of this approach for scalable combinatorial optimization, particularly in regimes where conventional discrete local search becomes computationally prohibitive.

papers.title: Faster and simpler traversal of 0/1-polytopes
papers.abstract: Recently, Merino and M\"utze (FOCS'23+SICOMP'24) presented an algorithm for computing a Hamilton path on the skeleton of any 0/1-polytope ${\rm conv}(X)$, where $X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n$. The algorithm uses as a black box an algorithm for solving the classical linear optimization problem $\min\{w\cdot x\mid x\in X\}$ for some weight vector $w\in\mathbb{R}^n$. The resulting delay per visited vertex on the Hamilton path is only by a $\log n$ factor larger than the time to solve one instance of the optimization algorithm. In this paper, we make the Hamilton path algorithm simpler and faster. Namely, we obtain an amortized delay that is only by a constant factor larger than the running time of the optimization algorithm, thus removing the $\log n$ factor. As concrete results, this yields improved algorithms for generating bases and independent sets in a matroid, spanning trees, forests, matchings and maximum matchings in a graph, vertex covers, minimum vertex covers, independent sets and maximum independent sets in a bipartite graph, and antichains, maximum antichains and ideals in a poset. All of these listings correspond to Hamilton paths on the corresponding polytopes. Furthermore, we obtain an $\mathcal{O}(t_{\rm LP})$ amortized delay algorithm for the vertex enumeration problem on 0/1-polytopes $\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid Ax\leq b\}$, where $A\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}^m$, and $t_{\rm LP}$ is the time needed to solve the linear program $\min\{w\cdot x\mid Ax\leq b\}$. This improves upon the $\mathcal{O}(t_{\rm LP} \log n)$ delay algorithm of Merino and M\"utze, and the previous $\mathcal{O}(t_{\rm LP}\,n)$ delay algorithm of Bussieck and L\"ubbecke from 1998.

papers.title: A simple algorithm for computing Hamilton paths on independent set polytopes
papers.abstract: The independent set polytope, or stable set polytope, of a graph $G$ is the 0/1-polytope defined by the convex hull of the characteristic vectors of all independent sets of $G$. We present a simple algorithm for computing a Hamilton path on the independent set polytope of a given $n$-vertex graph $G$ with amortized delay $\mathcal{O}(n)$. The independent sets are listed such that two consecutive sets differ either in removing a vertex, or adding a vertex and removing its neighbors from the independent set, i.e., the symmetric difference between two consecutive independent sets induces a star in $G$. As applications of this result, we obtain an algorithm to compute a Hamilton path on the matching polytope of an $m$-edge graph $G$ with worst-case delay $\mathcal{O}(m)$, which lists all matchings of $G$ in such a way that the symmetric difference between two consecutive matchings is a path on at most three edges. Furthermore, we obtain an algorithm to compute a Hamilton path on the chain polytope and order polytope of an $n$-element poset $P$ with amortized delay $\mathcal{O}(n)$, which lists all antichains of $P$ or all ideals of $P$, respectively, by star exchanges. Our algorithms are derived from the generic framework proposed by Merino and M\"utze (FOCS'23+SICOMP'24) for computing Hamilton paths on arbitrary 0/1-polytopes, which uses a linear optimization procedure as a black box. Our algorithms bypass solving the computationally intractable maximum weight independent set problem by a simple and purely combinatorial greedy rule.

papers.title: An ETH-based quasipolynomial lower bound for Dualization
papers.abstract: Dualizing monotone Boolean functions (or equivalently, enumerating minimal transversals in hypergraphs) is a long-standing problem whose output-polynomial-time solvability remains open. While various special cases have been extensively studied, the state-of-the-art algorithm for the general case, due to Fredman and Khachiyan, runs in quasipolynomial time. This paper presents a subexponential-time reduction from \textsc{3SAT} to the complement of \textsc{Dual}: Given a 3CNF formula with $n$ variables, the reduction constructs hypergraphs $H$ and $L$ of total size $2^{O(n^{2/3}(\log n)^{1/3})}$ such that $L \subseteq Tr(H)$ and the formula is satisfiable if and only if $L\neq Tr(H)$, where $Tr(H)$ is the set of minimal transversals of $H$. As a consequence of this reduction, assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), neither \textsc{Dual} nor \textsc{Dualization} admits an algorithm running in $N^{o(\sqrt{\log N/\log\log N})}$ time, where $N$ is the input size for \textsc{Dual} and the combined input and output size for \textsc{Dualization}. In particular, \textsc{Dualization} cannot be solved in output-polynomial time under ETH.
